title: Linking Words Loom
intro: However, although, despite, in spite of — weave the right connector into the sentence without breaking the logic or the grammar.

options: It was cold, so I wore a coat.
It was cold, but I wore a coat.
It was cold, so, I wore a coat.
A2.why: Cold, so a coat: “so” shows a result. The comma goes before “so”, not after.

options: I like tea, but I prefer coffee.
I like tea, so I prefer coffee.
I like tea but, I prefer coffee.
A2.why: Liking tea and preferring coffee contrast, so “but”, with the comma before it.

options: She was tired because she worked all day.
She was tired so she worked all day.
She was tired, because, she worked all day.
A2.why: “Because” gives the reason: she worked all day, so she was tired.

options: He studied hard, so he passed the exam.
He studied hard, but he passed the exam.
He studied hard so, he passed the exam.
A2.why: Studying hard led to passing: a result, so “so”. Comma before it, not after.

options: We stayed home because it was raining.
We stayed home so it was raining.
We stayed home, because, it was raining.
A2.why: The rain is the reason for staying home, so “because”, with no extra commas.

options: I wanted to go, but I was too tired.
I wanted to go, so I was too tired.
I wanted to go but, I was too tired.
A2.why: Wanting to go and being too tired pull in opposite directions: “but”.

options: It was late, so we went home.
It was late, but we went home.
It was late so, we went home.
A2.why: It was late, and the result was going home: “so”.

options: She smiled, and everyone felt happy.
She smiled, but everyone felt happy.
She smiled and, everyone felt happy.
A2.why: “And” simply adds the next event; “but” would need a contrast.

options: He was hungry because he skipped lunch.
He was hungry so he skipped lunch.
He was hungry, because, he skipped lunch.
A2.why: Skipping lunch is the reason he was hungry, so “because”.

options: The film was long, but it was very good.
The film was long, so it was very good.
The film was long but, it was very good.
A2.why: Long but good is a contrast: “but”, with the comma before it.

options: I was thirsty, so I drank some water.
I was thirsty, but I drank some water.
I was thirsty so, I drank some water.
A2.why: Thirsty, so water: “so” introduces the result, with the comma before it.

options: We went to La Malvarrosa because it was sunny.
We went to La Malvarrosa so it was sunny.
We went to La Malvarrosa, because, it was sunny.
A2.why: Sunshine is the reason for the beach trip, so “because”, with no commas round it.

options: It was raining. However, we went for a walk.
It was raining. Although, we went for a walk.
It was raining however we went for a walk.
B1.why: “However” starts the new sentence and takes a comma; “although” can't stand alone like that.

options: Although it was raining, we went for a walk.
Despite it was raining, we went for a walk.
Although it was raining we went, for a walk.
B1.why: “Although” is followed by a full clause; “despite” can't take a subject and verb.

options: Despite the rain, we went for a walk.
Despite of the rain, we went for a walk.
Despite the rain we went, for a walk.
B1.why: “Despite” takes a noun directly. Never “despite of”: that's “a pesar de” sneaking in.

options: In spite of the rain, we went for a walk.
In spite the rain, we went for a walk.
In spite of of the rain, we went for a walk.
B1.why: “In spite of” needs all three words; only “despite” goes without “of”.

options: He failed the exam. Nevertheless, he stayed positive.
He failed the exam. Despite, he stayed positive.
He failed the exam nevertheless he stayed positive.
B1.why: “Nevertheless,” begins a new sentence; “despite” needs a noun after it.

options: Although she was busy, she helped me.
Despite she was busy, she helped me.
Although she was busy she helped, me.
B1.why: A subject and verb (“she was busy”) follow “although”, not “despite”.

options: She passed the exam despite not studying much.
She passed the exam despite of not studying much.
She passed the exam although not studying much.
We continued the match in spite of the storm.
We continued the match despite of the storm.
We continued the match in spite the storm.
B1.why: “In spite of the storm” or “despite the storm”, but never “despite of”.

options: It was expensive. However, we bought it anyway.
It was expensive. Although, we bought it anyway.
It was expensive however we bought it anyway.
B1.why: “However,” at the start of a sentence links it to the one before.

options: Although the doctor was tired, he saw every patient.
Despite the doctor was tired, he saw every patient.
Although the doctor was tired he saw, every patient.
B1.why: A full clause (“the doctor was tired”) needs “although”, not “despite”.

options: Despite the heat, the cowboys rode all day.
Despite of the heat, the cowboys rode all day.
Although the heat, the cowboys rode all day.
B1.why: “Despite the heat”: a noun after “despite”, no “of”. “Although” needs a verb.

options: The paella was cold. However, everyone ate it.
The paella was cold. Although, everyone ate it.
The paella was cold however everyone ate it.
B1.why: “However,” opens the second sentence; “although” can't be used alone with a comma.

options: Sales rose in Asia, whereas they fell in Europe.
Sales rose in Asia, however they fell in Europe.
Sales rose in Asia whereas, they fell in Europe.
B2.why: “Whereas” contrasts two facts in one sentence; “however” can't join them with just a comma.

options: The plan failed. Consequently, the budget was cut.
The plan failed. Despite, the budget was cut.
The plan failed consequently the budget was cut.
B2.why: “Consequently,” starts a new sentence to show the result of the failure.

options: The report is thorough. Moreover, it is well written.
The report is thorough. Despite, it is well written.
The report is thorough moreover it is well written.
B2.why: “Moreover” adds a second positive point, after a full stop and with a comma.

options: He is talented. Furthermore, he works incredibly hard.
He is talented. Whereas, he works incredibly hard.
He is talented furthermore he works incredibly hard.
B2.why: “Furthermore” adds another point in the same direction: talented and hard-working.

options: I prefer tea. My sister, on the other hand, loves coffee.
I prefer tea. My sister, however the other hand, loves coffee.
I prefer tea my sister on the other hand loves coffee.
B2.why: “On the other hand” sits between commas in the middle of a sentence.

options: The team lost. Nevertheless, they remained confident.
The team lost. Whereas, they remained confident.
The team lost nevertheless they remained confident.
B2.why: Losing but staying confident is a contrast: “Nevertheless,” at the start of the sentence.

options: Costs rose sharply; consequently, prices increased.
Costs rose sharply; whereas, prices increased.
Costs rose sharply consequently prices increased.
B2.why: A semicolon before “consequently” and a comma after it link cause and result.

options: She is quiet, whereas her brother is very outgoing.
She is quiet, moreover her brother is very outgoing.
She is quiet whereas, her brother is very outgoing.
B2.why: “Whereas” contrasts two people in one sentence, with the comma before it.

options: The device is compact. Moreover, it is affordable.
The device is compact. Despite, it is affordable.
The device is compact moreover it is affordable.
B2.why: Compact and affordable are two good points, so “Moreover” adds the second.

options: Valencia is mild in winter, whereas Burgos is freezing.
Valencia is mild in winter, however Burgos is freezing.
Valencia is mild in winter whereas, Burgos is freezing.
B2.why: Two contrasting cities in one sentence: “whereas”, with the comma before it.

options: Antibiotics saved millions of lives. Moreover, they changed surgery for ever.
Antibiotics saved millions of lives. Despite, they changed surgery for ever.
Antibiotics saved millions of lives moreover they changed surgery for ever.
B2.why: “Moreover” adds a second, stronger point after a full stop.

options: The bank was robbed; consequently, the town hired a new sheriff.
The bank was robbed; whereas, the town hired a new sheriff.
The bank was robbed consequently the town hired a new sheriff.
B2.why: The robbery caused the hiring: “; consequently,” shows the result.

options: The event went ahead, notwithstanding the storm.
The event went ahead, notwithstanding of the storm.
The event went ahead notwithstanding, the storm.
C1.why: “Notwithstanding” works like “despite”: straight before the noun, with no “of”.

options: He accepted the offer, albeit reluctantly.
He accepted the offer, despite reluctantly.
He accepted the offer albeit, reluctantly.
C1.why: “Albeit” means “although”, and goes straight before an adjective or adverb.

options: The theory holds true insofar as conditions remain stable.
The theory holds true insofar that conditions remain stable.
The theory holds true, insofar as, conditions remain stable.
C1.why: The fixed phrase is “insofar as”, meaning “to the extent that”.

options: The results were disappointing. That said, there's room for improvement.
The results were disappointing. That say, there's room for improvement.
The results were disappointing that said there's room for improvement.
C1.why: “That said,” means “even so” and opens the second sentence with a comma.

options: Be that as it may, the decision stands.
Be that as it is, the decision stands.
Be that as it may the decision, stands.
C1.why: The fixed phrase is “Be that as it may”, meaning “even so”.

options: The strategy worked, albeit only in the short term.
The strategy worked, notwithstanding only in the short term.
The strategy worked albeit, only in the short term.
C1.why: “Albeit” adds a limit: it worked, though only for a short time.

options: Notwithstanding his objections, the plan was approved.
Notwithstanding of his objections, the plan was approved.
Notwithstanding his objections the plan, was approved.
C1.why: “Notwithstanding his objections”: no “of”, and the comma comes after the whole phrase.

options: The rule applies insofar as it doesn't conflict with local law.
The rule applies insofar that it doesn't conflict with local law.
The rule applies, insofar as it doesn't conflict, with local law.
C1.why: “Insofar as” introduces a condition; don't split it off with commas.

options: It was a small victory. Be that as it may, it mattered.
It was a small victory. Be that as it is, it mattered.
It was a small victory be that as it may it mattered.
C1.why: “Be that as it may” is fixed, never “as it is”, and it takes a comma.

options: The treatment was effective, albeit painful.
The treatment was effective, notwithstanding painful.
The treatment was effective albeit, painful.
C1.why: “Albeit” goes straight before the adjective: “albeit painful”.

options: Notwithstanding the drought, the harvest in the huerta was good.
Notwithstanding of the drought, the harvest in the huerta was good.
Notwithstanding the drought the harvest, in the huerta was good.
The town was lawless. That said, most settlers lived peacefully.
The town was lawless. That say, most settlers lived peacefully.
The town was lawless that said most settlers lived peacefully.
C1.why: “That said,” concedes a point after a full stop: lawless, yet mostly peaceful.
